flagged.evidence: The page says every representation is the Hilbert sum of its 'finite-dimensional irreducible isotypic components'. Take the trivial compact group acting trivially on ℓ²(N). Its sole isotypic component is the whole infinite-dimensional, reducible space. The scoped decomposition theorem correctly states that each nonzero isotypic component is a possibly infinite Hilbert sum of copies of a finite-dimensional irreducible.

The page describes a unit L² vector 'whose modulus is invariant under all translations — and such an L¹ class vanishes almost everywhere'. The modulus has not been established to belong to L¹. For example, v(x)=(1/2)(1+|x|)^(-3/4) has L² norm one but nonintegrable modulus, showing that the unit-vector hypothesis supplies no such inclusion. The opened vanishing lemma explicitly supplies the valid bridge: 'apply the first statement to g=|v|²∈L¹'. The counterexample item uses that bridge correctly.

[F3] says 'R(K) is the linear span of the matrix coefficients of finitely many finite-dimensional continuous unitary representations'. For K=T, any fixed finite collection of such representations has a finite-dimensional coefficient span, of dimension at most the sum of their squared dimensions. But R(T) contains all the infinitely many linearly independent integer characters, as verified in the scoped circle example. The opened definition instead says that each individual representative function is a finite linear combination; it does not supply one finite collection spanning R(K).

After choosing φ₀ with φ₀(e)=1 and vanishing outside U, the step asserts that its symmetrization has 'support in U'. The opened support definition is supp f=closure({x:f(x)≠0}), so vanishing outside an open set does not imply this. On K=R/Z take U=(-1/10,1/10), g=[2/5], and φ₀([t])=max(1-10|t|,0), using representatives t∈[-1/2,1/2]. These satisfy the prescribed conditions and g∉U+U; φ₀ is already symmetric, but supp φ=[-1/10,1/10] contains boundary points outside U. The opened Urysohn statement licenses vanishing outside U, not the asserted support inclusion. Only the weaker vanishing property is needed subsequently.

After deriving m<n²S for nonempty finite subsets, the step concludes 'every finite subset of F_n has fewer than n²S elements'. Take a singleton index set with its vector equal to zero. Then S=0 and F_n=∅, whose finite subset ∅ has cardinality zero; the asserted strict bound becomes 0<0. The opened square-summable-family definition explicitly includes the empty finite subset. The strict conclusion must retain the nonempty qualification, or use a non-strict bound for arbitrary finite subsets.
